# Preface {.unnumbered}

A gene is not a transcript. Most human genes produce several, sometimes dozens,
and the differences between them are often the biology. Which protein domain is
present, which cell type expresses which form, whether a transcript is
translated at all or routed to decay: these are isoform-level questions, and a
gene-level answer cannot reach them.

Yet most transcriptomic analysis still collapses this to one number per gene.
That collapse is sometimes justified and often simply inherited from a time when
nothing finer was measurable. This book is an argument, built from the primary
literature, that the finer resolution is where a great deal of the biology lives.

It is organized as a book rather than a tool list because the case is cumulative:
landmark examples across the tree of life, the technology arc that made them
visible, the disease biology that depends on isoform-level resolution, and the
current efforts to catalog the isoform universe outright.

::: {.callout-note}
## Status
All chapters are drafted and none has had a second reader. Every chapter is
built from line-anchored claim records, and four mechanical gates run on every
commit: recorded quotes are re-read from the source, chapter prose is checked
against those quotes for overlap, every cited number is checked against the
claim it cites, and the bibliography is regenerated from the records rather
than edited. [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) explains how, and why it is
built that way.

Four glossary terms rest on no citable source and are marked in place as the
book's own. They are the entries most in need of review.
:::
